questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: Rules are keyword if and ID=[a-z]+. Longest match is used, with keyword priority on equal lengths. How is if tokenized?

options.label: A lexical error due to ambiguity

questions.explanation: Both rules match length two; the explicitly stated priority selects the keyword.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: With ID=[a-z]+, INT=[0-9]+, PLUS='+', and skipped spaces, what is the token sequence for x+12?
questions.explanation: The plus is its own token, and maximal munch groups both digits into one integer lexeme.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: Which fact distinguishes lexeme from token type?

options.label: A lexeme is always an integer value.
x and count can share type ID while having different lexemes.
Each token type has exactly one spelling.
Token types must preserve every source-space character.

questions.explanation: A category can have many spellings. Lexemes are concrete source substrings, while types identify categories.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: With INT=[0-9]+ and value conversion to decimal, what may the token for 007 contain?

options.label: Three separate tokens under maximal munch
Type ID because of the leading zeros
Value 007 as a different mathematical integer from 7
Type INT and value 7, optionally retaining lexeme "007"

questions.explanation: The lexical rule accepts the digit run. A semantic value and original spelling may both be stored, and their representations need not match.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: Why should ordinary repeated token rules avoid matching ε?

options.label: They can emit tokens without advancing the input, causing an infinite loop.
A DFA can never accept ε.
ε cannot be described by a regex.
Every ε match must be a syntax error.

questions.explanation: A zero-length token needs special handling. Otherwise a scanner can repeatedly succeed at the same input position.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: In a nested-switch scanner, what do the outer and inner switches typically inspect?

options.label: Current state, then input character or character class

questions.explanation: The two switches implement the two arguments of δ: state and symbol.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: In a table-driven scanner, what does T[s][index(c)] store?

options.label: The next state from state s on character c

questions.explanation: Rows select current states and columns select symbols or equivalent character classes.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: For n states and m individually indexed input symbols, what is the transition table size?
questions.explanation: One cell is needed per state-symbol pair. Additional token-type metadata may be stored separately.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: What does 'ad hoc' mean in the implementation choices shown?
questions.explanation: Both switch-based and table-based scanners can be handwritten. The label concerns how the implementation is produced.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: What does a scanner generator consume in the lecture's model?

options.label: Token regular expressions and associated actions

questions.explanation: The generator creates recognition code and invokes specified actions when token patterns match.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: Why might a large DFA favor a table-driven implementation?

options.label: Tables require no handling of invalid input.
Its transitions can be stored and generated systematically.

questions.explanation: Table-driven code separates transition data from control flow. It still needs memory, indexing and error handling.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: Suppose reading '+' ends an identifier x but '+' starts the next token. What must scanning do?

options.label: Append '+' to the identifier regardless of its rule.
Restart from the beginning of the file.
Preserve or push back '+' for the next token.

questions.explanation: Lookahead that is not part of the current lexeme must remain available to the next scan.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: If a tentative longer token fails after the scanner has passed an accepting state, where should maximal munch end?

options.label: At the first accepting position always.
At the furthest examined position regardless of validity.
At the last accepting position, restoring later characters.
At the start of the file.

questions.explanation: The longest valid prefix may be shorter than the longest path explored. Remember the last accepting state and input position.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: What must happen at end of file if a valid token is pending?

options.label: Discard it because no delimiter followed.
Add an imaginary delimiter to its lexeme.
Emit the token before reporting end of input.

questions.explanation: EOF can terminate a token. A scanner that only emits on delimiters will lose the final token.

questions.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
questions.question: Can an ordinary DFA minimization merge accepting scanner states for ID and INT solely because both accept?

options.label: Only if the scanner is generated, then always yes.
Yes; token values do not matter to a parser.
No; distinct observable token outputs must be preserved.
Yes; every final state is equivalent.

questions.explanation: Recognition-only equivalence preserves a Boolean answer. Scanner minimization must also preserve token types/actions and applicable priorities, so initial classes must respect outputs.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: Which four statements are equivalent?

options.label: L is nonregular; L has an NFA; L has a parser; L has a scanner.
L has a regex; L has exactly one DFA; L has exactly one NFA; L is finite.
L is regular; some RE describes L; some NFA recognizes L; some DFA recognizes L.
L is finite; every NFA recognizes L; every DFA recognizes L; L={ε}.

questions.explanation: The theorem is about existence of equivalent descriptions for the same language, not finiteness or uniqueness.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: What does equivalence between an RE and a DFA mean?

options.label: They run equally fast in every implementation.
They specify or accept exactly the same words.
They have the same number of symbols and states.

questions.explanation: Language equality is the invariant across representations. Structure and resource costs can differ.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: Why does every DFA have an equivalent NFA immediately?

options.label: Treat each DFA destination as a singleton successor set and use no ε moves.
Add an ε edge between every pair of states.

questions.explanation: A DFA already satisfies the more permissive NFA model once its deterministic transitions are written as singleton sets.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: Which pipeline is the standard construction taught for compiling token patterns?
questions.explanation: Recursive NFA construction handles regex operations, subset construction removes nondeterminism, and minimization merges equivalent states.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: Which construction converts an NFA to a DFA?
questions.explanation: Subset construction stores sets of NFA states as DFA states. State elimination is the route from an automaton to an RE.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: Which construction converts an NFA to an RE?

options.label: Treat it as a GNFA and eliminate states while preserving path languages.
Treat every state name as a literal input word.
List only words of length at most |Q|.

questions.explanation: Generalized edges summarize all possible paths through removed states. A finite sample or single path misses other accepted words.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: Does the theorem mean every language has a regular expression?

options.label: Yes; every language has finite words.
No; only regular languages do in this formal sense.
Yes; every language has an alphabet.
Only if the language is infinite, then yes.

questions.explanation: Nonregular languages such as {0^n1^n:n≥0} have no formal regular expression or finite-automaton recognizer.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: Why is there no one-to-one correspondence between individual regexes and languages?

options.label: a, a|a and εa all describe {a}.
Every regex denotes an empty set.
A language must have infinitely many symbols.

questions.explanation: The recursive definitions correspond in their constructors, but several syntactic descriptions can denote the same set.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: Can minimizing an equivalent DFA change whether ε is accepted?

options.label: Yes; ε is ignored by equivalence.
No; minimization preserves the language including ε.
Only when the NFA had ε transitions.

questions.explanation: Empty-word membership is part of language equality. The class containing the start state must have the correct accepting status.

questions.title: The equivalence theorem
questions.question: What does exponential DFA blow-up say about expressive power?

options.label: Every NFA necessarily produces all 2^|Q| subsets.
Nothing stronger for NFAs; it concerns description size, not which languages exist.

questions.explanation: Equivalent DFAs always exist, but some languages have much more compact NFAs. Worst-case growth is an upper bound and can be necessary, not universal.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: How do GNFA edge labels differ from ordinary NFA labels?

options.label: They may only be final-state names.
They must be entire input files.
They may be arbitrary regular expressions.

questions.explanation: Ordinary NFA labels are one symbol or ε; GNFA labels can summarize multi-symbol path languages.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: What does a GNFA edge labeled ab* consume?

options.label: One a followed by zero or more b symbols

questions.explanation: The label is interpreted as a regex. For instance a, ab and abb can traverse the edge.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: What regex represents no edge between two GNFA states?
questions.explanation: No edge means there is no consumable word connecting that ordered pair. ε would add an empty-word path.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: Parallel edges labeled R and S can be replaced with which label?
questions.explanation: A path can take either edge. Concatenation would require traversing both sequentially, which is a different structure.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: Why add a new sole final state with ε edges from old final states?

options.label: It forces every word to contain ε as a symbol.
It preserves every accepting path while giving a single elimination endpoint.

questions.explanation: Existing accepted words can finish by one ε move. Old accepting states cease to be accepting in the normalized machine.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: Why add a fresh start with an ε edge to the old start in strict GNFA normalization?

options.label: It forces the old start to be rejecting on every suffix.
It consumes a mandatory input symbol.
It creates a start with no incoming edges without changing the language.

questions.explanation: The fresh start provides a clean endpoint for elimination. The old start remains as an ordinary state and can be eliminated.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: If the old start is also final, how does normalization preserve ε?

options.label: It must add a literal symbol ε to Σ.
It must delete ε from the language.
It cannot normalize such an automaton.
The new start reaches the old start and then the new final by ε moves.

questions.explanation: The empty run through the original automaton becomes an ε-only path between the new endpoints.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: Does an edge labeled ∅* permit a traversal?

options.label: Yes; it consumes the printed symbol ∅.
No; any label containing ∅ blocks all paths.

questions.explanation: ∅* denotes {ε}. Distinguish the empty language label ∅ from its star.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: If a GNFA has only a start s and final f with label R from s to f and no other nonempty-language edges, what is its language?
questions.explanation: The only accepting traversal uses the s-to-f edge once, consuming a word described by R.

questions.title: Generalized NFA
questions.question: The lecture also allows a final two-state GNFA with loops and a return edge. Can its s-to-f label alone always be the answer?

options.label: No; such a GNFA cannot have a regex.
Yes; final states stop all input consumption.
No; the remaining loops and return cycles must also be included.
Yes; all loops can be deleted.

questions.explanation: Strict fresh-endpoint normalization avoids these remaining edges. Otherwise use a two-state formula accounting for every possible cycle.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: Which formula eliminates q between remaining states i and j?
questions.explanation: A path either avoids q using the old edge or enters q, loops zero or more times, and exits. Input order must be preserved.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: Edges i→q:a, q→q:b, q→j:c, i→j:d are present. What replaces i→j after deleting q?
questions.explanation: The old direct path d remains, and paths through q consume a, any number of b symbols, then c.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: If q has no self-loop, what does its loop factor become?
questions.explanation: No self-loop still permits zero repetitions, so paths through q remain possible. Replacing the loop factor by ∅ would incorrectly erase them.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: If i→q has label ∅, what new contribution comes from paths through q?
questions.explanation: It is impossible to enter q from i, so the concatenated contribution is empty. The old i-to-j edge is still retained.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: Why must elimination consider i=j?

options.label: A state cannot have a self-loop in a GNFA.
Paths through q may create or enlarge a self-loop on i.
i=j forces the whole language to be empty.

questions.explanation: Eliminating an intermediate state can expose a cycle returning to the same remaining state. Ignoring it loses repeatable paths.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: Edges i→q:ε, q→q:a, q→j:b|ε, i→j:∅. What is the new label?
questions.explanation: Simplify ∅|εa*(b|ε) to a*(b|ε). The exit can consume b or nothing, and the loop can be traversed zero times.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: If two correct elimination orders produce different-looking regexes, what must hold?

options.label: Their operators occur in the same order.
One of them must be wrong.

questions.explanation: The preserved object is the accepted set of words, not expression syntax or size.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: In a two-state GNFA, s has loop A, s→f label B, f→s label C, and f has loop D. What is a correct full regex?
questions.explanation: First reach f via A*B. At f, repeat either a local D loop or an excursion C back to s followed by A*B. s and f are distinct and only f is final.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: With s-loop 0, s→f label 1, f→s label 0 and f-loop 1, what does the formula yield?
questions.explanation: Substitute A=0,B=1,C=0,D=1. Returns from f can be followed by arbitrary extra zeros at s before returning on 1.

questions.title: Collapsing a GNFA
questions.question: What is a sound way to disprove equivalence of two candidate regexes?

options.label: Give one word matched by exactly one expression.
Show both match ten selected words.

questions.explanation: A single membership disagreement disproves set equality. Matching finite samples does not prove equality for all words.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: What does one subset-construction DFA state represent?

options.label: All NFA states possible after one input prefix

questions.explanation: Nondeterministic alternatives become a single set-valued summary handled deterministically.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: What is the DFA start state for an ε-NFA?
questions.explanation: ε transitions may be taken before any input symbol, so the initial possible-state set must include the full closure.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: When is a subset S final?

options.label: When every member of S is final

questions.explanation: One original accepting state supplies an accepting NFA path after the prefix.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: An NFA has n states. What is the general upper bound on subset DFA states?
questions.explanation: Each DFA state is a subset of the n original states. Only reachable subsets need be retained, so the actual number can be much smaller.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: Suppose s --ε→ p, p --a→ q, q --ε→ f; f is final and all other transitions are absent. What is the first DFA transition on a?
questions.explanation: The start closure is {s,p}. Taking a reaches q, then closure adds f; previous states are not retained unless reached again.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: An NFA has only s --ε→ p, p --a→ q, q --ε→ f; f is final. From active set {q,f}, what happens on the next a?
questions.explanation: Neither q nor f has an a transition. Subset construction recognizes one whole word and does not restart a scanner automatically.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: When should the empty subset be included in the constructed DFA?

options.label: Never; a DFA cannot have a state represented by ∅.
When it is reachable, or when explicitly completing a transition to it.
Only if the NFA start is final.

questions.explanation: The empty subset is a valid state label meaning no live NFA paths. It loops to itself on every symbol and is nonfinal.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: NFA: s loops on 0 and 1 and s --1→ f, with only f final and no other edges. How many reachable subset states occur?
questions.explanation: The reachable sets are {s} and {s,f}. s is always present because of its loops, so ∅ and {f} alone are unreachable.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: Does subset construction guarantee a minimal DFA?

options.label: Only when every subset is reachable, then always yes.
No; different reachable subsets may be equivalent.
Only when ε transitions occur, then always yes.
Yes; subsets are automatically equivalence classes.

questions.explanation: Subset construction removes nondeterminism. Minimization is a separate operation comparing future acceptance behavior.

questions.title: Subset construction
questions.question: When does the iterative reachable-subset procedure stop?

options.label: When every discovered subset has processed transitions on every symbol and no new subset appears.
When the first accepting subset appears.
When the empty subset first appears.

questions.explanation: All reachable transitions must be explored. Discovering acceptance or a dead subset does not finish the other branches of the worklist.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: When are two DFA states equivalent?

options.label: They agree on acceptance for every possible continuation.
They have the same incoming edge count.
They have the same printed name length.

questions.explanation: Equivalence is a universal condition on future suffixes. Current final status is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: What is a distinguishing string for states p and q?

options.label: Any word containing two different symbols
A word reaching both from the start
A suffix accepted from exactly one of them

questions.explanation: The same suffix must produce different acceptance outcomes when started in the two states.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: Which string distinguishes any accepting state from any nonaccepting state?

options.label: Only a word of length two

questions.explanation: With no input, each state retains its own final status, which already differs.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: If p and q are both final, must they be equivalent?

options.label: No; a later suffix may distinguish them.
Only if p is the start, then yes.
Yes; all final states must merge.
Only if the alphabet is binary, then yes.

questions.explanation: They agree on ε but may disagree after one or more symbols.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: If p and q transition on a into states already known to be distinguishable, what follows?

options.label: a must be removed from the alphabet.
Their a destinations must be merged.

questions.explanation: If suffix w distinguishes the destinations, aw distinguishes p and q.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: Does having identical destination names on every symbol and equal final status suffice for equivalence?

options.label: Only if both states are sinks
No; incoming edges must also match.

questions.explanation: After one symbol both runs are in the same state; ε is handled by equal final status. Incoming edges are irrelevant to continuation behavior.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: Can equivalent states have different immediate destination names?

options.label: Yes, if corresponding destinations are themselves equivalent.
Only if the states are unreachable.
Only if every destination is final.

questions.explanation: Equivalence concerns destination behavior, not literal names. Partition refinement compares destination classes.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: If p∼q and q∼r, what follows?

options.label: p and r must be distinct final states
p and r must have no transitions

questions.explanation: Agreement on acceptance for every suffix is transitive, as well as reflexive and symmetric.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: Two nonfinal states cannot reach any final state. Are they equivalent?

options.label: Only if their outgoing edges are identical.
Only if both are unreachable from q0.
Yes; every suffix is rejected from both.

questions.explanation: Their right languages are both empty. Different rejecting internal structures can collapse into one dead class.

questions.title: Equivalence classes
questions.question: Which observation is insufficient to prove equivalence?

options.label: They have equal final status and identical transitions to the same states.
A stable accepting-status-respecting partition puts them in one block.
Both states reject every tested suffix of length at most two.

questions.explanation: A distinguishing suffix may be longer than the limited test set. The other conditions supply general arguments, not just bounded examples.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: What is the standard initial partition for recognition-only DFA minimization?

options.label: One block for each input symbol
F and Q\F, omitting empty blocks

questions.explanation: ε immediately separates final from nonfinal states. Start status is not the acceptance distinction used for initial refinement.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: What should be removed before computing the minimal reachable DFA?
questions.explanation: Unreachable states cannot affect any input run. Reachable sinks or loops may be essential.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: What triggers splitting a current block?

options.label: Two of its states have transitions on one symbol into different current blocks.
Two states have different incoming edge counts.
The block contains the start state.

questions.explanation: Distinct destination behavior can distinguish the source states. State names and how a state was reached do not define equivalence.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: With blocks N={p,q} and F={r}, p --a→ p and q --a→ r, what must happen?

options.label: Keep p and q together because both are nonfinal.

questions.explanation: After suffix a, p stays nonfinal while q reaches a final state. That one-symbol witness distinguishes them.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: If a refinement round makes no splits, what follows?

options.label: The original DFA had the smallest number of named states.
The partition is stable under all symbols if every block and symbol was checked.

questions.explanation: Stability means no further distinguishing behavior remains within the blocks. The original may have redundant states that are now merged.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: Where is the start state in the quotient DFA?

options.label: The class containing the original q0

questions.explanation: Each original run is mapped to classes; its initial state must map to the class containing q0.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: How are quotient transitions defined?

options.label: Use incoming edges instead of outgoing edges
Pick any class regardless of q

questions.explanation: Stability ensures all representatives of [q] have a-successors in the same class, so the transition is well-defined.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: What is the minimal complete DFA for ∅ over a nonempty alphabet?

options.label: One nonfinal state looping on every symbol
Two states, one final and one nonfinal
One final state with no edges

questions.explanation: A DFA must have a start state. A single rejecting sink recognizes ∅ and is minimal.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: Does minimization always strictly reduce the number of states?

options.label: Yes; at least one state must disappear.
Yes; the result always has two states.
Only for infinite languages, then always yes.
No; an already minimal reachable DFA stays the same size.

questions.explanation: Minimization finds the smallest equivalent state count; it need not be smaller than the input count.

questions.title: DFA minimization
questions.question: What is meant by uniqueness of the minimal complete DFA for a fixed language and alphabet?

options.label: A unique set of state names
A unique order of partition-refinement steps
Unique up to consistent state renaming

questions.explanation: Isomorphic minimal reachable complete DFAs have the same structure and behavior after renaming. Drawings and execution of the algorithm may differ.
